extracted.intended_audience: CCS project developers, coal-fired power plant owners/operators, UIC permit applicants, state/tribal regulators, and other stakeholders responding to EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: EPA Class VI and CCS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Exegesis of EPA's final rule preamble describing requirements, expectations, timelines, and procedural steps for Class VI UIC permitting, geologic sequestration projects, and the compliance date/timeline for CCS on long‑term coal-fired steam generating units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and project decision schedules for Class VI applications
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA Regions will classify all Class VI well applications received on or after December 12, 2023, as applications for major new UIC injection wells and develop project decision schedules for reviewing Class VI permit applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal guidelines streamline and create uniformity and consistency in the Class VI permitting process and set target timeframes for components of the permitting process (e.g., number of days Regions should set for public comment periods, developing responses to comments, and final permit decisions). These measures are intended to reduce permitting timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target throughput: EPA review timeframe for complete Class VI applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA aims to review complete Class VI applications and issue permits when appropriate within approximately 24 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timeframe is dependent on project complexity and the quality and completeness of the submitted application. Applicants should submit a complete application and provide any information requested by the permitting agency in a timely manner so as not to extend the overall time for the review. Incomplete or insufficient application materials trigger NODs/RAIs and back-and-forth review that can substantially delay permitting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency via Class VI permit tracker
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA maintains a Class VI permit tracker showing information for projects that have submitted Class VI applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracker fields include current permit review stage, whether a project has been sent a Notice of Deficiency (NOD) or Request for Additional Information (RAI), and the applicant's response time to any NODs or RAIs. The tracker supports transparency about permit status.

rubrics_metrics.name: State primacy application phases
rubrics_metrics.description: States may apply to the EPA for primacy to administer Class VI programs; the primacy application process has four phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four phases are: (1) pre-application activities, (2) completeness review and determination, (3) application evaluation, and (4) rulemaking and codification. Successful primacy can reduce the number of permits in EPA review and leverage state expertise/capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity-building resources for permit writers and regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has created resources including training series and guidance documents to build capacity for Class VI permitting for both permit writers and regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resources and internal guidelines are intended to create uniformity and streamline permitting. The IIJA established a $50 million grant program to support states, Tribes, and territories in developing and implementing UIC Class VI programs; EPA allocated specified amounts to jurisdictions that submitted letters of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of sequestration capacity at commercial scale
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's position that commercial geologic sequestration capacity is growing and adequate to support the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites multiple commercial facilities in construction or advanced development with proposed sequestration capacities ranging from 0.03 to 6 million tons CO2/year and ongoing Class VI permit reviews in multiple states; anticipates more sites responding to financial incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) via GHGRP subparts RR and VV
rubrics_metrics.description: GHGRP subpart RR and subpart VV regulations prescribe accounting methodologies for facilities to quantify and report any potential leakage at the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA makes sequestration data and related monitoring plans publicly available on its website. The rule requires any affected unit that employs CCS and injects captured CO2 underground to report under GHGRP subpart RR or subpart VV. If an emitting EGU sends captured CO2 offsite, it must transfer the CO2 to a facility that reports in accordance with GHGRP subpart RR or VV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to demonstrate injection will not endanger USDWs and to monitor/mitigate induced seismicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the UIC Class VI program, EPA requires mechanisms to identify, monitor, and mitigate risks associated with induced seismicity and requires applicants to demonstrate induced seismic activity will not endanger USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include site characterization and monitoring; further analyses, planned operational changes, and additional monitoring may be required if geologic/seismic data indicate a substantial likelihood of seismic activity. EPA has authority to require seismic monitoring as a permit condition or to deny a permit if injection-induced seismicity risk could endanger USDWs. EPA also provides practical approaches for UIC Directors to minimize/manage injection-induced seismicity (including discretionary conditions under Class II where appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class II vs Class VI permit trigger and protections for USDWs
rubrics_metrics.description: Class II wells (including ER wells) are for fluids associated with oil and gas production; operations that shift to geologic sequestration must obtain a Class VI permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA disagrees that Class II ER wells are necessarily less protective of human health than Class VI wells; however, the regulations require the operator of a Class II well to obtain a Class VI permit when operations shift to geologic sequestration (40 CFR 144.19). UIC Class VI regulations require owners/operators to show sufficient injection zone volume and to report any fluid migration out of the injection zone and into or between USDWs (40 CFR 146.83 and 40 CFR 146.91).

rubrics_metrics.name: Site suitability and reporting of fluid migration
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/operators must show the injection zone has sufficient volume to contain the injected CO2 stream and must report any fluid migration out of the injection zone and into or between USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited regulatory provisions: 40 CFR 146.83 and 40 CFR 146.91. Reporting and monitoring expectations are part of permit conditions to ensure containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-injection site care (PISC) and long-term financial responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Class VI regulations impose requirements after injection ceases, including plugging, PISC, and site closure obligations; default PISC period is 50 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During PISC the permittee must monitor the CO2 plume and pressure front and demonstrate USDWs are not endangered (40 CFR 146.93). Permittee must maintain financial responsibility to cover plugging, corrective action, emergency and remedial response, PISC, and site closure until permitting authority approves site closure (40 CFR 146.85(a)&(b)). Even after fulfilling UIC obligations, a former permittee may be liable for previous regulatory noncompliance; EPA may issue orders necessary to protect public health (42 U.S.C. 300i; 40 CFR 144.12(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for meaningful engagement with overburdened communities and environmental justice expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA acknowledges the importance of meaningful engagement with local, historically disadvantaged, and overburdened communities and has programs and public participation requirements to support this process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's environmental justice guidance for Class VI permitting and primacy contains expectations broadly applicable across injection well classes; Regions should apply them to other classes, including Class II, wherever possible. See section VII.C.1.a.i(D)(4) for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal sufficiency for early CCS projects and pore space/ liability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA disagrees legal uncertainties (pore space ownership, long‑term liability) preclude CCS development; existing legal frameworks and state laws address pore space ownership and liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interagency CCS task force concluded early projects could proceed under existing frameworks. BLM ROWs and policy address Federal pore space on BLM lands. Many states have statutes/regulations clarifying pore space ownership and are enacting laws addressing long-term liability; EPA does not believe these issues will delay implementation beyond discussed timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date for long-term coal-fired units and extension mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes a compliance date of January 1, 2032 for long-term coal-fired steam generating units subject to a CCS BSER and provides a mechanism for a 1-year compliance date extension in cases where delays are outside a source's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The compliance date justification assumes limited feasibility work during state plan development, followed by substantial work after state plan submission, yielding ~6 years and 7 months for CCS installation. Additional factors considered include FEED/baseline schedules and real-world project experience (Boundary Dam Unit 3, Petra Nova). States may adopt different compliance schedules accounting for particular circumstances (see section X.C.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed project timeline for CCS components (capture, storage, pipeline)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's baseline schedule assumptions for CCS deployment on existing coal units, including durations and sequencing for capture plant, storage site, and pipeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture plant: feasibility up to 1 year (June 2024–June 2025), FEED study 1 year (June 2026–June 2027), commercial arrangements ~9 months, permitting 1 year, engineering & procurement ~2 years, sitework ~6 months, construction ~2 years, startup & commissioning ~14 months; EPA indicates reasonable minor compressions are possible. Storage: up to 3 years for final site characterization, pore-space acquisition, permitting (including at least 2 years for Class VI permitting), plus 1 year construction. Pipeline: up to 3 years for final routing/permitting/ROW acquisition, plus 1.5 years for construction. These timelines are used to support the January 1, 2032 compliance date but may be adjusted in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA timing considerations for CCS projects
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA does not assume CCS projects are generally subject to NEPA, but NEPA may be triggered in specific circumstances and has timing implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEPA review is required when federal funding is received, for projects on federal lands, or where other federal permits (e.g., Clean Water Act section 404) trigger NEPA. If applicable, an EA of ~1 year can be finalized concurrently with permitting periods; an EIS could take ~2 years concurrently. NEPA review may begin prior to completion of a FEED study in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement for early engagement with permitting authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA encourages applicants to contact their permitting authority early to gain a thorough understanding of the Class VI permitting process and the permitting authority's expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early engagement helps applicants avoid incomplete/substandard applications that lead to NODs/RAIs and delays. EPA maintains a list of UIC contacts within each EPA Regional Office on the Agency's website and has met with many companies and stakeholders to assist applicants.
